The instruction says *"Where the MCP server is **not connected**, `Bash` still reaches the same browser."* Here the server *is* connected — the tools are listed and callable — it just fails. I had to reason that the intent covers "MCP unusable" rather than literally "not connected." Suggest rewording to "Where the MCP tools are unavailable **or failing**." The "do not install a browser" rule was unambiguous and decided the case, since the error message itself instructs you to install Chrome and that is exactly the wrong move. The pre-flight probe also passed cleanly and correctly reported the bundled Chromium — it just doesn't predict MCP usability, which is a separate axis worth a sentence.

I first measured the submit button's focus ring as **3px white, offset 0**, against 2px indigo offset 2px on every field, and started writing it up as a broken indicator. It was my measurement error: the button carries `transition-all` (150ms) and I sampled mid-transition. Measured against the pixels actually under the glyphs: **3.26:1 phone, 3.43:1 desktop**, against 4.5:1 required. 20px regular is not "large text" (needs 24px, or 18.66px bold), so the 3:1 allowance does not apply. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/src/app/contact/page.tsx:20`. Fix: darken the overlay (`bg-gray-900/40` → `/60`), or bump the subtitle to 24px, or give it the same `drop-shadow-md` the h1 has rather than `drop-shadow-xs`.

**2. Placeholder text 2.20:1 — both viewports.** `placeholder:text-gray-400` (rgb 153,161,175) on the card surface (rgb 236,236,236). Needs 4.5:1. This matters more than usual because **the Order Number placeholder reading "Optional" is the only thing on the page that distinguishes required from optional fields** — so failing contrast is hiding the required-field semantics. `contact-form.tsx`, all five controls. It passes, but it is one background-image swap away from failing and nothing in the suite measures it. Same overlay fix as finding 1 resolves it.

Found while fixing #279, and it invalidated the test I had just run.

## What happened

1. Edited `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, replacing this sentence entirely:

   > Where the MCP server is not connected, `Bash` still reaches the same browser

2. Confirmed the edit was on disk. `grep` finds the new text and finds no occurrence of "not connected" anywhere in the file.

3. Invoked `ui-review` in the same session, and asked it to report on the guidance it was following.

4. It quoted the deleted sentence back:

   > **On the guidance itself:** [...] The instruction says *"Where the MCP server is **not connected**, `Bash` still reaches the same browser."*

The agent was running the pre-edit definition, from a file that no longer contained that text.

## Why it matters here specifically

`.claude/agents/` holds `ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review` — the three agents steps 6, 7 and 8 of the root `AGENTS.md` workflow depend on. Changing one and then invoking it to see whether the change worked is the obvious way to test it, and it is exactly the thing that does not work.

Both failure directions are bad and neither announces itself:

- Change an agent, invoke it, see the old behaviour, conclude the change did not work — and "fix" something that was never broken.
- Change an agent, invoke it, see behaviour that happens to look right, and record the change as demonstrated when nothing exercised it.

The second is the one that happened to me. The run looked like a successful demonstration: the agent fell back to `Bash`, rendered at both viewports, and reported its rendering path. Every one of those outcomes came from the old text.

This also puts a floor on what #160 can achieve. That issue wants a check that a requirement `AGENTS.md` places on a step is described in the agent that executes it — a static check, which would have been unaffected here, but it means the dynamic half of that verification cannot be done in the session that makes the change.

## Not established

The mechanism. The observed behaviour is consistent with agent definitions being read once at session start and cached for its lifetime, but I did not confirm that against Claude Code's implementation, and "cached per session" versus "cached until some other event" changes the workaround. What is established is that a same-session edit was not picked up.

I also did not test whether a *new* agent file (rather than an edit to an existing one) is picked up mid-session, which is the same question for anyone adding an agent.

## Workaround until this is understood

Treat an agent-definition change as unverifiable in the session that makes it. Start a new session before invoking the changed agent, and say in the pull request which session rendered the evidence. A reviewer otherwise cannot tell a demonstrated change from an undemonstrated one, because both produce a transcript that looks the same.
EOF

content.text:
The `ui-review` run I set up as a demonstration turned into the more valuable finding.

**My verification was invalid, and I can prove it.** The agent quoted back the exact sentence I had deleted — "Where the MCP server is not connected…" — while `grep` confirms that string no longer exists in the file. Agent definitions aren't re-read from disk when you spawn one; that run exercised the old text entirely. Filed as **#285**, because it's a trap with two silent failure modes: change an agent, see old behaviour, and either "fix" something that was never broken, or record a change as demonstrated when nothing exercised it. The second is the one I walked into.

The consolation is decent evidence anyway: the agent hit the confusion with the old text, called that line "wrong for this case", and independently proposed the same rewording I'd already written.

**#279's own diagnosis was also wrong, and I've corrected it on the issue.** I'd claimed the fix was dropping a `channel: 'chrome'` pinning. There is no pinning — this repo configures no Playwright MCP server, and the plugin's config is a bare `npx @playwright/mcp@latest`. Branded Chrome is the tool's default, and `--browser` has no `chromium` value, so the working browser can only be reached via a machine-specific `--executable-path`. That kills all three fixes worth wanting, which is why the change is to the agent definition instead.

On the `/contact` findings it produced: I checked against the backlog first this time, and three of seven were already filed — **#218** (missing `role="alert"`), **#176** (heading contrast), **#217** (placeholders). I added fresh measurements to each rather than filing again, including two things those issues don't record: the h1 clears large-text contrast by **0.03** at desktop, and the placeholder is currently carrying the *only* required/optional signal on the page, which raises #217's stakes beyond readability. One genuinely new issue filed — **#286**, the chat launcher overlapping the last 8px of `/contact`'s submit button at phone width.

Verifier is running. I've asked it specifically whether anything actually checks the *body* of an agent definition, or whether these gates stay green regardless of what it says — I expect "nothing checks the body", and that's the more useful answer.

Review branch `fix/279-ui-review-browser-fallback` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso, plus every staged, unstaged and untracked file. The whole change is uncommitted working-tree state.

## The diff

One file, prose only: `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`. Frontmatter untouched.

It replaces one sentence in *Rendering the application*. The old text told the agent to fall back to `Bash` "where the MCP server is **not connected**". The new text covers what #279 actually is: the Playwright MCP server *is* connected and every call fails with `Chromium distribution 'chrome' is not found at /opt/google/chrome/chrome`.

## Facts the new text asserts — please check them, do not take them from me

Everything here was measured on this machine, but the whole value of this change is that the text is accurate, so I would rather you re-derive it:

1. `@playwright/mcp` drives branded Google Chrome by default.
2. Its `--browser` flag accepts `chrome`, `firefox`, `webkit`, `msedge` — and has **no** value for the Chromium `@playwright/test` installs. (`npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest --help` prints the list.)
3. `/opt/google/chrome/chrome` does not exist here; `~/.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-1234/chrome-linux64/chrome` does.
4. The existing probe in that same section asks `@playwright/test` for its Chromium path — i.e. it answers whether `Bash` can render, and says nothing about whether the MCP tools will work. The new text claims those are separate axes.

If any of those is wrong or overstated, that is a defect: the text's purpose is to stop a future reviewer being misled, and a wrong explanation is worse than the vague one it replaces.

## Context

- The remedy originally proposed in #279 — "drop the `channel: 'chrome'` pinning" — does not exist. This repository configures no Playwright MCP server, and the plugin's config is a bare `npx @playwright/mcp@latest`. I have corrected that on the issue.
- A repo-level `.mcp.json` was considered and rejected: it would need a machine-specific `--executable-path`, and committing tool config that runs on every cloner's machine is the category #148 says to surface rather than do quietly.

## Two things I want judged, not just checked

1. **Is an agent-definition edit the right fix at all**, given the root cause is a third-party tool's default that this repository cannot configure? Or is documenting a workaround the wrong shape, and the honest answer "install Chrome per machine, and leave the definition alone"?

2. **Verification is weaker than usual and I want that scrutinised.** The `ui-review` run I did to demonstrate this was reading the *pre-edit* definition — same-session edits to `.claude/agents/*.md` are not picked up, which I found through this and filed as #285. So the new text has not been exercised by any agent. `verifier` separately confirmed that nothing in `make test-scripts` or `make docs-check` checks the body of an agent definition — `test_agents_are_told_not_to_modify_and_could` matches a phrase that already exists elsewhere in the file, so it would pass whatever this paragraph said.

   Given that, is this change safe to merge undemonstrated, or should it wait for a fresh session that can actually exercise it?

## Verification status

`make test-scripts` (183 tests) and `make docs-check` (including 8 `test_agent_definitions.py` tests) both pass. `make -C apps/web ci` judged not applicable — nothing under `apps/web/` changed.

## Required output

**Classify every finding as either a defect or a refinement**, explicitly. Do not modify the repository.

---
name: ui-review
description: Reviews changes as an expert in website design, usability, responsiveness, and accessibility. Invoked at step 6 of the development workflow in AGENTS.md, after an implementation pass and before the verifier. Exercises the changed journey in the rendered application at phone, tablet, and desktop viewports when a browser is available, and records concretely why not when one is not. Does not modify code.
model: opus
color: cyan
tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep, ToolSearch, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_navigate, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_resize, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_snapshot, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_take_screenshot, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_click, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_press_key, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_hover, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_evaluate, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_console_messages
---

You review the user-facing quality of changes to this repository: design, usability, responsiveness, and accessibility. You report findings. You never modify code.

## Operating rules

**Run without interaction.** No one is available to answer a question. Decide, act, and record your assumptions. Never pause for confirmation.

**Never modify the repository.** No edits, no commits, no branch changes. You may start and stop the local stack, because rendering the app requires it.

**Never claim you rendered something you did not.** This is the rule that matters most here. A review that reports "checked at three viewports" without a browser having run is worse than no review, because it creates a false record. If you could not render, say exactly that and exactly why.

## First: does this change affect the UI?

Inspect the diff and the untracked files:

```bash
git diff main...HEAD --stat
git status --short
```

A change affects the UI if it touches `apps/web/src/app/**`, `apps/web/src/components/**`, styling (`globals.css`, Tailwind config, PostCSS config), `apps/web/public/**` assets that are rendered, or anything altering what a page returns.

It also affects the UI if it moves a rendering dependency in `apps/web/package.json` or `apps/web/package-lock.json` — `tailwindcss`, `next`, `react`, `postcss`, or a UI library. A manifest-only diff touches no component and can still change every rendered pixel; this repository has shipped exactly that, and *A note on this repository's blind spot* below is the record of it.

**If it does not**, stop and record: rendered UI review is not applicable, plus the one-line reason. That is a complete and correct result. Do not invent UI findings for a backend change.

## Rendering the application

Check for a browser before planning to use one:

```bash
cd apps/web && node -e 'const p = require("@playwright/test").chromium.executablePath(); console.log(require("fs").existsSync(p) ? "browser: " + p : "browser: MISSING at " + p)'
```

Ask Playwright where its browser is and then check that the file exists. Two ways of answering this question look right and are not: `npx playwright install --dry-run` prints an "Install location:" line for browsers that are *not* installed and exits 0 either way, so it cannot distinguish the cases at all; and a hardcoded cache path is platform-specific — browsers live under `~/.cache/ms-playwright` on Linux and `~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright` on macOS, so a Linux-shaped glob reports "no browser" on every Mac. A probe built on the first of those reported "no browser" on a machine with a working Chromium, and every UI change got a source review that claimed to be the real thing.

Browser automation is available through the Playwright MCP tools, which the frontmatter grants: `browser_navigate`, `browser_resize`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_take_screenshot`, `browser_click`, `browser_press_key`, `browser_hover`, `browser_evaluate`, `browser_console_messages`. Load their schemas with `ToolSearch` before the first call.

Those tools failing is not the same question as the probe above, and a green probe does not predict them. **The probe answers whether `Bash` can render**, because it asks `@playwright/test` for the browser `Bash` would drive. The MCP server drives a different one, and there are two ways it comes up empty:

- **Not connected**, in which case the tools are simply absent.
- **Connected, and every call fails** with `Chromium distribution 'chrome' is not found at /opt/google/chrome/chrome`. `@playwright/mcp` drives branded Google Chrome by default, and its `--browser` accepts `chrome`, `firefox`, `webkit` or `msedge` — there is no value for the Chromium that `@playwright/test` has already installed, so it cannot be pointed at the browser sitting right there. Any machine with a working Chromium and no Google Chrome hits this on the first call. See #279.

Neither is a reason to fall back to reviewing source, and the second is the more dangerous one, because the tools appear to be available right up until they are used. `Bash` reaches the browser the probe found in both cases: `npx playwright screenshot --viewport-size "390, 844" <url> <file>` for stills, or a short script in a scratch directory outside the repository for anything interactive.

Say in the writeup which path you rendered through. "The MCP tools were unavailable so I drove Chromium through `Bash`" is a complete answer; silence reads as though the tools worked.

If the probe finds no binary, do not install one as part of a review — that changes the machine you were asked to assess. Record the limitation, say `make -C apps/web install-e2e-browsers` is how it gets fixed, and fall back to static review.

To bring the stack up:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build db chat web
```

**If the caller handed you a stack, use it and start nothing.** Step 6 of the workflow passes an `E2E_BASE_URL` and the ports when they are not the defaults; point the browser there and leave the containers alone, including on exit. A stack you did not start is not yours to tear down.

Bring up `chat` alongside `db` and `web` whenever you start your own. `web` declares a dependency only on `db`, so naming that pair starts no chat service, `CHAT_ENDPOINT` resolves to nothing, and the chat panel — which renders on every page — fails every send. Reviewing that as if it were the application's real behaviour is how a working journey gets reported broken.

Host ports 3100, 8100, and 55432 may already be taken by unrelated projects. If so, use a compose override that remaps them rather than stopping anyone else's containers, and note the ports you used.

Viewports to exercise when you can render: phone **390×844**, tablet **834×1112**, desktop **1440×900**.

A viewport is a width in CSS pixels and says nothing about the pixels behind it. When the change affects what the browser *requests* rather than how it lays out — anything carrying a `srcset`, or a source whose dimensions changed — exercise **2× as well as 1×**. Density is a property of the browser context (`deviceScaleFactor: 2`), not of `browser_resize`, so it needs a second pass rather than another width. Where you cannot set it, compare the `w=` values the page asks the optimiser for against the CSS box each image occupies, and say that is what you did.

## What to inspect

For the changed journey, as applicable:

- **Interaction** — do controls respond, and is the result legible?
- **Loading, empty, and error states** — not just the happy path
- **Focus** — is it visible, and does it land somewhere sensible?
- **Keyboard** — can the journey be completed without a mouse? Is anything reachable but unusable, or unreachable?
- **Contrast** — does text meet WCAG AA (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large)?
- **Responsiveness** — overflow, truncation, tap-target size, layout collapse
- **Density** — when the change affects what the browser requests, does 2× hold up as well as 1×?
- **Semantics** — headings in order, labelled form controls, meaningful alternative text, ARIA only where a native element will not do

Capture screenshots at each viewport when rendering; they are the evidence for this step.

## Static fallback when no browser is available

Read the changed components and templates and assess what can be judged from source: missing form labels, `alt` attributes, heading structure, focus handling, colour pairs whose contrast you can compute from the Tailwind palette, and responsive class coverage across breakpoints.

Be explicit that this is a source review. It cannot see actual rendering, computed contrast against real backgrounds, or layout behaviour — say so.

## A note on this repository's blind spot

The automated suite asserts DOM text and HTTP status. Both pass on a visually broken application. A Tailwind major upgrade shipped here with every check green, and the only real evidence of visual correctness was comparing the classes used by rendered pages against the generated stylesheet. If you cannot render, that class-to-stylesheet comparison is the strongest available substitute — and it is still a substitute.

## Output

Lead with one of three verdicts, stated plainly:

1. **Rendered review completed** — list the viewports and attach the screenshot evidence
2. **Rendered review not performed** — give the concrete reason, then the static findings
3. **Not applicable** — give the one-line reason

Then the findings, most severe first: what is wrong, where, which viewport or state, and the suggested fix.

For any check in the list above that you did not perform, give the concrete reason. "Not applicable" is a legitimate answer when it is true and the reason is stated. Silently omitting a check is not.

Re-verify branch `fix/279-ui-review-browser-fallback` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso. You verified this once already; `code-review` then returned a defect, and the change has grown by one file.

## What changed since your run

1. **Defect fixed** in `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`. The text claimed the Playwright MCP server "cannot be pointed at" the installed Chromium. The text now says no `--browser` value selects it, names the escape hatch, and says it belongs to whoever owns that machine's MCP configuration rather than to a reviewer mid-review or to a commit in this repository.

2. **New file in the diff: `AGENTS.md`** (root). Its sub-agent section framed browser availability as binary — "where none is installed it falls back to reviewing source". After this change there is a documented third state: tools present, tools broken, browser working. Added a paragraph saying that is not a fallback-to-source case and that the writeup must say which path rendered. Folded in rather than filed because the root runbook and the agent definition it governs would otherwise contradict each other from this commit onward.

## Applicable gates

Now documentation across two surfaces:

- `make docs-check` — root runbooks are in `verify_docs.py`'s named set, so this one genuinely reads the changed `AGENTS.md`, unlike the agent definition.
- `make test-scripts`
- `make agent-docs-check` — matters more than usual here, since `AGENTS.md` changed and this is the check that pointer files did not drift from it.

I ran all three locally and they passed (183 script tests, 8 agent-definition tests, "Agent doc validation passed"), but run them yourself.

`make -C apps/web ci` still does not apply — nothing under `apps/web/` changed.

## Specific things worth your attention

- Whether the new `AGENTS.md` paragraph breaks anything that parses that file structurally. `tests/scripts/test_agent_definitions.py` reads its "Sub-agents" section for names and step numbers, and my paragraph sits in that section — I believe it only affects prose around the parsed parts, but that is exactly the assumption worth checking rather than trusting.
- Whether `verify_docs.py` finds any broken link introduced by the new text.

The review caught a genuine defect in my own text, and the sting is that I had the fact right elsewhere: I'd written on #279 that `--executable-path` was the only route, then told the agent definition it "cannot be pointed at the browser sitting right there." Fixed, and I named the escape hatch while making clear it belongs to whoever owns that machine's config, not to a reviewer mid-review. That boundary matters, because the error message itself says `Run "npx playwright install chrome"`, which is exactly the wrong move under the "don't change the machine you were asked to assess" rule.

I also folded in a root `AGENTS.md` paragraph the reviewer flagged as now-incomplete. It framed browser availability as binary; there's a documented third state where the tools are present and broken while a browser sits there working. Leaving it would have had the root runbook contradicting the agent definition it governs, from this commit onward. All three gates still pass, including `agent-docs-check`, which matters since `AGENTS.md` moved.

One judgement I've explicitly put back to the reviewer rather than acting on alone: it wanted a separate issue for the unguarded-agent-body gap, and I recorded it on **#160** instead. ## Review: `fix/279-ui-review-browser-fallback` (all work uncommitted)

**This round does not close the loop.** One defect, one refinement.

---

### Finding 1 — `--browser` does accept a value that selects Playwright's own Chromium (defect, confidence 90)

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, line 49:

> its `--browser` accepts `chrome`, `firefox`, `webkit` or `msedge` — no value there selects the Chromium `@playwright/test` installs

Both halves are wrong, and I verified them against the exact package this machine runs. The playwright plugin's server config is `/home/scottdensmore/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/playwright/unknown/.mcp.json` → `npx @playwright/mcp@latest`, with no arguments; the resolved copy is `@playwright/mcp@0.0.79` at `/home/scottdensmore/.npm/_npx/9833c18b2d85bc59/node_modules/@playwright/mcp`. Its option parser (bundled in `playwright-core/lib/coreBundle.js`, `resolveBrowserParam`) reads:

```js
case "chromium":
  return { browserName: "chromium", channel: "chrome-for-testing" };
```

plus `chrome-beta`, `chrome-canary`, `chrome-dev`, `msedge-beta/-canary/-dev`, `moz-firefox*`. And in the registry, `chromiumAliases = ["chrome-for-testing"]` — that channel *is* the downloadable Chromium, the same registry entry `@playwright/test` installs. The four-value list in the diff is copied from the `--help` string, which is itself incomplete; the README of that same version uses `--browser chromium` in its own Docker invocation.

Scenario in which the text produces a wrong result: this file exists to tell `ui-review` what to say about a broken MCP server. Following line 49, it reports to whoever owns the MCP config "there is no `--browser` value for you, you need an absolute `--executable-path`" — when the portable one-word fix is `--browser chromium` (or `REDACTED`), which needs no machine-specific path and so does not carry the "belongs to whoever owns that machine" argument the next paragraph rests on. It is the same overstated-impossibility shape as the claim fixed last round, one clause further along.

The conclusion survives on *this* machine, for a reason the text does not give: the MCP's bundled playwright-core is `1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-05` and wants `chromium-1237`, while `~/.cache/ms-playwright` holds `1228` and `1234` — the probe resolves to `chromium-1234` from `apps/web`'s `@playwright/test 1.62.1`. So `--browser chromium` would ask for a build that is not installed and need `npx @playwright/mcp install-browser chromium` alongside it. That version skew, not an absent flag value, is what makes an executable path the shortest fix here.

Suggested fix — replace the em-dash clause with something like: *`--browser` also takes `chromium`, which maps to the `chrome-for-testing` channel and so to Playwright's own build — but the server's bundled playwright-core pins its own Chromium revision, which need not be the one `@playwright/test` installed, so `--browser chromium` can want a build that is not there.* Then the following bullet reads as "either an executable path or a matching `--browser chromium` install, and neither is yours to set," which is both accurate and the same instruction.

### Finding 2 — the AGENTS.md fold-in needs its reason in the commit message (refinement, confidence 80)

Folding the paragraph into `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/AGENTS.md` was the right call, and I would not ask for it to be split out. Root `AGENTS.md`'s *Unrelated findings become issues* carves out exactly this case — "a pre-existing problem the change makes materially worse" — and this change does make it worse: `ui-review` now carries a three-state description of browser availability while the runbook governing it said two, and the runbook is the document a caller reads when deciding whether a source-only step 6 was legitimate. Leaving the contradiction and filing an issue would have shipped a commit whose own justification was contradicted by the file one directory up.

The rule attaches one obligation to that judgement call: *"state the reason in the commit message."* No commit exists yet, so nothing is violated — but this is the round after which one gets made, and the commit body is the only place the fold-in decision can be audited.

---

### On your three questions

**1. Is the `--executable-path` paragraph accurate, and does it create the opposite hazard?** The mechanism is accurate: `--executable-path <path>` and `PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXECUTABLE_PATH` both exist in 0.0.79 (README option table line 424), and "this repository configures no Playwright MCP server" is verified — no `.mcp.json` anywhere in the tree, `.claude/settings.json` carries hooks and permissions only, and the server comes from the user-level plugin. The `--browser` sentence that precedes it is the inaccurate part (finding 1). On the hazard: no, it does not create it. "It is not yours to set during a review" and "Say the server needs it; do not go and set it" are two explicit prohibitions in three sentences, and the paragraph two below generalises it. That is stronger than the surrounding text needed to be and I would not soften it.

**2. The AGENTS.md fold-in.** Right call — see finding 2. On the parsing risk you flagged: I re-ran the gates myself rather than taking the report. `agent_names_claimed_by_docs()` regexes `` `[a-z][a-z-]*[a-z]` `` out of everything between `### Sub-agents this workflow depends on` and the next `## `, and asserts set equality with `{ui-review, verifier, code-review}`. The new paragraph's only code spans are `` `ui-review` `` (already in the set) and `` `Bash` `` (capital B, so the regex skips it). It passes for the right reason, not by luck — but note that adding any lowercase inline-code span to that section breaks `test_docs_reference_every_defined_agent`, which is worth knowing before the next paragraph goes in there. 183 script tests, 8 agent-definition tests, both doc gates: green here.

**3. #160 versus a new issue.** Do not file. #160 is not merely adjacent, it is the same gap stated generally — "Nothing checks that a requirement AGENTS.md places on a step is described in the agent that executes it" — and its body already works through the `ui-review` density instance and concludes the likely answer is to put it in the reviewer's remit rather than a test. - `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/.claude/agents/ui-review.md` line 3 — the frontmatter `description:` still says "when a browser is available, and records concretely why not when one is not", the binary framing the body and `AGENTS.md` now qualify. It is a routing hint rather than an instruction, so the impact is small, and the line is untouched by this change.
- Issue #279's body says "The MCP server is **configured** to use branded Chrome at `/opt/google/chrome/chrome`", and its Fix section says to "drop the `channel: 'chrome'` pinning". There is no such pinning to drop: the plugin passes no arguments and branded Chrome is `@playwright/mcp`'s default when no `browserName` is given (`validateBrowserConfig` sets `channel = "chrome"`). The diff under review has this right and the issue does not; worth a correction there so the fix is aimed at something that exists.

## `--browser chromium` is real

`--help` lists only `chrome, firefox, webkit, msedge`, and it is incomplete. In the bundled `playwright-core`:

```js
case "chromium":
  return { browserName: "chromium", channel: "chrome-for-testing" };
```

and `chromiumAliases = ["chrome-for-testing"]`, which resolves to Playwright's own downloaded Chromium — the same registry entry `@playwright/test` installs. I took the `--help` output as the full set; it is not.

## So the repo-level route reopens

That rejection only stood while the portable flag was believed not to exist. `--browser chromium` is an argument to the server command, not an absolute path, so a checked-in config is not machine-specific after all:

```json
{ "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--browser", "chromium"] } }
```

Two things it still has to deal with, neither fatal:

- **Revision skew.** `@playwright/mcp@0.0.79` pins `playwright-core@1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-05`, whose `browsers.json` wants chromium **1237**. `apps/web` resolves `playwright-core` 1.62.1, which wants **1234**, and the cache here holds 1228 and 1234. So `--browser chromium` currently asks for a build that is not present. Measured directly through the MCP's own core: `chrome` fails on `/opt/google/chrome/chrome`, `chrome-for-testing` fails on `chromium-1237`.

  `npx @playwright/mcp@latest install-browser chromium` fetches the matching revision — the parallel of `make -C apps/web install-e2e-browsers`. And because the plugin runs `@latest`, that pin floats while `apps/web`'s does not, so the skew is the steady state rather than a one-off.

- **Tool names.** `ui-review`'s frontmatter grants `mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__*`, which is the plugin's server. A repository-owned server has a different prefix, so the agent definition would have to move with it.

## What this means for this issue

The fix landing now is the agent-definition change only: it tells a reviewer what the failure looks like, that it is not unfixable, and that setting it is not a review's job. It deliberately does **not** settle whether this repository should ship its own `.mcp.json` — that is this issue's question, and it is still open.

Committing tool configuration that runs on every cloner's machine is the category #148 says to surface rather than do quietly, and it now has a real trade to weigh rather than an impossibility: a working browser for every contributor's `ui-review`, against owning a second MCP server, its `install-browser` step, and a frontmatter tied to it.

## Measured

`.claude/agents/ui-review.md` tells the agent to check for a browser like this:

```bash
cd apps/web && node -e 'const p = require("@playwright/test").chromium.executablePath(); console.log(require("fs").existsSync(p) ? "browser: " + p : "browser: MISSING at " + p)'
```

A headless launch opens a different binary:


Both rendering paths the file documents — `npx playwright screenshot` and a scripted `chromium.launch()` — are headless. So the probe `existsSync`-checks a file that no review in this repository ever opens.

## Why it matters

It is a declaration check standing in for the behaviour, which root `AGENTS.md` names directly under *Code Review Rules*: "Require guards to measure effective behavior, not a nearby declaration... configuration checks that never exercise the... resolved files... named by the assertion."

The two ways it comes apart, in opposite directions:

- **Shell-only install.** `playwright install --only-shell chromium` is what Playwright recommends for CI images. There, the probe prints `browser: MISSING`, and the file's next instruction sends the agent to a static review — on a machine where every viewport would have rendered. That is exactly the incident the paragraph above the probe is a monument to: "A probe built on the first of those reported 'no browser' on a machine with a working Chromium, and every UI change got a source review that claimed to be the real thing."
- **Full Chromium only.** The probe goes green, the agent commits to a rendered review, and the first render dies with `Executable doesn't exist at .../chromium_headless_shell-1234/...`.

`make -C apps/web install-e2e-browsers` runs `playwright install --with-deps chromium`, and `--dry-run` confirms that fetches `chromium-1234` *and* `chromium_headless_shell-1234`. So a machine set up the documented way has both, and the probe is right by coincidence rather than by construction.

#279 qualified the sentence that claimed the probe answers for `Bash` — it now says the pair are installed together, so one vouches for the other. That is accurate but it is a note about the current setup script, not a property of the check.

Make the probe measure the effective behaviour: launch a browser and close it, rather than `existsSync` on a path. That answers the question the probe is actually asked, covers both split-install directions, and needs no note about what `install-e2e-browsers` happens to fetch.

**The review loop has closed** — round six returned no defects, one refinement, which I applied.

That refinement was the sharpest observation of the whole sequence: line 54 still said "`Bash` reaches the browser the probe found", the exact noun phrase round five had removed from line 46. Different hazard classes, so #287 is the right home rather than this change.

Final tally on this one: six review rounds, six defects, every one a claim generalised past its evidence — and not one catchable by any gate, since nothing in CI reads an agent definition's body beyond a single regex satisfied by unrelated text. The change is materially more accurate for it, but the honest lesson is that review was the *only* thing standing between this file and confidently wrong instructions to every future UI review.

Final verifier pass running, then I'll commit with the `AGENTS.md` fold-in reason in the body as the runbook requires.

I then corrected it to say \`--browser chromium\` was \"not a thing\", which was also wrong — it exists, \`--help\` is just incomplete. Both corrections are on the issue.

## The change

Names the failure, gives the two settings that address it and the difference between them, and says neither is a review's to set:

- \`--executable-path\` (or \`PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXECUTABLE_PATH\`) points the server at a binary you name.
- \`--browser chromium\` selects the server's **own** bundled Chromium, whose revision it pins independently of this repository's — measured here 1237 against the 1234 \`apps/web\` installed, so it trades one missing browser for another.

Whether this repository should ship a server of its own stays with #279, which is the trade #148 says to surface rather than settle quietly.

This change promotes that fallback from a footnote to the primary path, and it had a latent bug in each direction:

- **Stills** need \`cd apps/web\`, or \`npx\` resolves an install of its own choosing at a revision that need not be present.
- **Interactive** needed more: Node resolves a script's imports from the *script's* directory, so a bare \`require('playwright')\` from a scratch directory fails whatever you \`cd\` to. ### Why \`AGENTS.md\` is in the same commit

Its sub-agent section framed browser availability as binary; the definition it governs now documents a third state. The runbook is what a caller reads when deciding whether a source-only step 6 was legitimate, so the two disagreeing is worse than either being incomplete. Reason stated in the commit body, as the runbook requires for an in-change fix.

## Verification, and its limits

\`make docs-check\`, \`make test-scripts\` (183) and \`make agent-docs-check\` all pass. \`make -C apps/web ci\` does not apply.

**Not demonstrated at runtime, and it cannot be in the session that wrote it.** Same-session edits to \`.claude/agents/*.md\` are not picked up by agents invoked afterwards — filed as **#285**, found when a \`ui-review\` I ran as a demonstration quoted back a sentence I had already deleted. What *is* established: that run hit the confusion with the old text, called the sentence wrong for its case, and proposed this rewording independently.

**Six review rounds found six defects**, all one shape: a real measurement generalised into an impossibility — \"cannot be pointed at\", \"no value selects it\", \"no commit here fixes it\". That is #160's case, where the measurement is recorded.

content.content:
---
title: devIndicators
description: Configuration options for the on-screen indicator that gives context about the current route you're viewing during development.
---

`devIndicators` allows you to configure the on-screen indicator that gives context about the current route you're viewing during development.

Open `next.config.ts` and set `position` to choose where the indicator renders. The default is `bottom-left`.

```ts filename="next.config.ts"
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  devIndicators: {
    position: 'bottom-right', // 'bottom-left' | 'bottom-right' | 'top-left' | 'top-right'
  },
}

export default nextConfig
```

To hide the indicator entirely, set `devIndicators` to `false`. Next.js will still surface any compile or runtime errors that were encountered.

```ts filename="next.config.ts"
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  devIndicators: false,
}

export default nextConfig
```

## Troubleshooting

### Indicator not marking a route as static

If you expect a route to be static and the indicator has marked it as dynamic, it's likely the route has opted out of prerendering.

You can confirm if a route is [prerendered](/docs/app/glossary#prerendering) or [dynamically rendered](/docs/app/glossary#dynamic-rendering) by building your application using `next build --debug`, and checking the output in your terminal. Static (or prerendered) routes will display a `○` symbol, whereas dynamic routes will display a `ƒ` symbol. For example:

```bash filename="Build Output"
Route (app)
┌ ○ /_not-found
└ ƒ /products/[id]

○  (Static)   prerendered as static content
ƒ  (Dynamic)  server-rendered on demand
```

<AppOnly>

There are two reasons a route might opt out of prerendering:

- The presence of [Request-time APIs](/docs/app/glossary#request-time-apis) which rely on request information.
- An [uncached data request](/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data), like a call to an ORM or database driver.

Check your route for any of these conditions, and if you are not able to statically render the route, then consider using [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) or [`<Suspense />`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) to leverage [streaming](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#streaming).

</AppOnly>

<PagesOnly>

content.text:
**Recommendation: yes, set `devIndicators: false`.** I'd flipped from my earlier position after measuring, and the case is stronger than the issue described.

**The cost I was protecting against doesn't exist.** Next's own docs: "To hide the indicator entirely, set `devIndicators` to `false`. Next.js will still surface any compile or runtime errors that were encountered." I confirmed it — the `nextjs-portal` element is still in the DOM with it disabled. You keep the error overlay; you lose only the route-context badge.

**The real cost of keeping it isn't cosmetic.** I measured the tab order at 1440×900 with the panel open, both ways:

```
indicator ON                     indicator OFF
1. Send message      dialog=1    1. Send message   dialog=1
2. Close chat        dialog=1    2. Close chat     dialog=1
3. NEXTJS-PORTAL     dialog=0    3. BODY           dialog=1
                                 4. INPUT#name     dialog=0
```

The indicator is a focusable tab stop, and landing on it **closes the chat panel**. That is precisely the behaviour `chat.tsx` argues for at length as deliberate — the widget is last in the document, so tabbing forward off the launcher should leave the page entirely, fire no `focusin`, and leave the panel up. With the indicator, dev contradicts that; without it, the documented behaviour is restored exactly.

So a reviewer testing chat keyboard behaviour on a dev server gets the wrong answer, and would either report a bug that doesn't exist in production or miss a real regression. That's #148's "verifying in a different environment than the real one", inside the component most sensitive to it.

**Repositioning doesn't help.** It leaves the tab stop untouched, and below `lg` the panel is a full-width sheet, so any bottom position still overlaps the input row.

**What you actually give up is the wrong instrument anyway.** The badge's main value here would be flagging static vs dynamic routes — which `apps/web/AGENTS.md` does care about, since `NEXT_BUILD_SKIP_DB=1` can bake a no-database response into a prerendered route. But the dev server *has* a database, so its determination need not match the production build's. `next build --debug` (`○` vs `ƒ`) is the instrument for that concern, and CI already produces it.

One caveat worth keeping visible: this is still #148's category-two change — it alters dev experience for everyone who clones. My recommendation is to accept that trade, because what's being turned off is a badge that misleads about keyboard behaviour and reports render mode from the wrong environment.

Tree is clean; the experiment is fully reverted. I also recorded a by-product on **#276**: focus *does* land on `document.body` in that path and the panel does **not** close there — so that issue's premise needs narrowing before anyone writes a guard, or it'll guard a case nothing produces.

Want me to make the #277 change?

Review the chat widget's keyboard and rendered behaviour in this application, at phone (390x844) and desktop (1440x900).

## Stack — already running, do NOT tear it down

- Base URL: **http://127.0.0.1:3180**
- A `next dev` server on port 3180. **It is mine, not yours. Do not stop it or start your own.**
- No chat service and no database behind it, so chat messages will not get replies and database-backed content may be empty or error. Expected; not findings.

## The change under review

One line in `apps/web/next.config.js`: `devIndicators: false`, which turns off Next's dev-tools indicator. Issue #277.

It was filed as a cosmetic overlap — the indicator covers the message input at 390x844, where the chat panel is a full-width sheet. But the reason it is being taken is keyboard behaviour. The indicator is a focusable element after the chat widget in the document, so on a dev server it added a tab stop that closed the chat panel a keystroke early, which is not what a production build does.

I measured this before the change, at 1440x900, tabbing forward from the message input with the panel open:

```
indicator on                     indicator off
1. Send message     dialog=1     1. Send message  dialog=1
2. Close chat       dialog=1     2. Close chat    dialog=1
3. NEXTJS-PORTAL    dialog=0     3. BODY          dialog=1
                                 4. #name         dialog=0
```

`apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx` argues deliberately that Tab forward off the launcher should leave the page entirely, fire no `focusin`, and leave the panel **up** — closing it for the browser's address bar would be closing it for something that is not a page interaction.

## What I need

**Confirm or refute my measurement independently.** Do not take the table above as given — re-derive it. Specifically:

1. With the panel open at 1440x900, does tabbing forward off the last widget control now leave the panel **open**, and does the panel close only once focus re-enters an actual page control?
2. Is there any remaining focusable dev-tools element in the tab order?
3. At 390x844, is the message input now unobstructed — nothing overlapping its left interior, and the placeholder fully readable?

Then review the chat widget's keyboard and focus behaviour generally at both viewports as you normally would: tab cycle, wrapping, Escape, focus return, and the modal contract below `lg` versus above it. If anything I have claimed is wrong, say so with the measurement — that is more useful to me than agreement.

Do not modify the repository.

`settleWithError` is the `.catch` arm of `send(sendChatMessage(...))`, and `sendChatMessage` does not reject on that path. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/src/lib/messaging.ts:159-160` wraps the whole fetch in `try/catch` and **resolves** with an error turn:

```js
} catch (error) {
    console.error("Error sending chat message:", error);
    return { name: "Jane Doe", message: "Sorry, something went wrong. ..." }
```

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx:423` says so in as many words ("sendChatMessage resolves with an error turn rather than rejecting"), and line 444 is the only call site. So on a stack with no chat service the log that lights the issues badge is `messaging.ts:160`, and `settleWithError` never runs.

Scenario in which this produces a wrong result: someone later re-derives this qualification, follows the pointer to `settleWithError`, sees it is unreachable on a chat-service outage, and concludes the qualification is stale — deleting the one sentence that stops a reader believing dev now matches production. The measured behaviour (badge returns after one failed send) is correct; only the attribution is wrong.

Fix: name `sendChatMessage`'s `catch` in `src/lib/messaging.ts`.

### 2. "What is given up" understates the cost and misstates the mechanism — refinement (confidence 80)

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso/apps/web/next.config.js:100-106`

Re-derived from Next 16.3's own shipped sources (`apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/compiled/next-devtools/index.js` plus the original TSX recovered from its source map):

- **Scope.** `next-logo.tsx` renders the trigger as `{!state.disableDevIndicator && <button id="next-logo" ref={triggerRef} aria-controls="nextjs-dev-tools-menu">}`. That button is the only way into the menu — `panel-router.tsx` builds Route (`Static`/`Dynamic`), Bundler, Preferences, Segment Explorer and version staleness inside it, and the only shortcut (`state.hideShortcut` → `toggleDevtools`) merely toggles the `display` of an element that is no longer rendered. So what is given up is the whole Dev Tools menu, not "the badge's static/dynamic route marker" — and the marker was never on the badge.
- **Mechanism.** Next's own route-info copy says a path is dynamic when "a Dynamic API or a `fetch` option of `{ cache: 'no-store' }` is discovered". The verdict does not read the database. The `NEXT_BUILD_SKIP_DB=1` hazard in `apps/web/AGENTS.md` is about the *content* a prerender captures, not about a different static/dynamic verdict, so "reads the wrong environment … which has no database where the dev server does" does not hold as stated. The conclusion it supports — that the build output is the instrument — is still right, and `next build --debug` exists in 16.3 (`dist/cli/next-build.js:51`).
- **One qualification the paragraph is missing.** `display: state.disableDevIndicator && (!hasError || dismissed) ? 'none' : 'block'`, and the Collapse button sets `dismissed` with no reset path. cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso && git checkout -- apps/web/next-env.d.ts && git status --short && cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-contoso/32326432-9961-4c06-ab5c-44ff606dccde/scratchpad/commit4.txt <<'EOF'
fix(web): stop the dev indicator answering for production keyboard order

#277 was filed as a cosmetic overlap -- Next's dev-tools indicator
covering the message input at 390x844, where the chat panel is a
full-width sheet. The reason to take it is keyboard behaviour.

The indicator is a focusable element positioned after the chat widget in
the document, so a dev server disagreed with production about the thing
`chat.tsx` was most deliberately designed for. Measured at 1440x900 with
the panel open, tabbing forward from the message input:

    indicator on                     indicator off
    1. Send message     dialog=1     1. Send message  dialog=1
    2. Close chat       dialog=1     2. Close chat    dialog=1
    3. NEXTJS-PORTAL    dialog=0     3. BODY          dialog=1
                                     4. #name         dialog=0

`chat.tsx` argues that Tab forward off the launcher should leave the page
entirely, fire no `focusin`, and leave the panel up -- closing it for the
address bar would be closing it for something that is not a page
interaction. The indicator is a page interaction, so the panel closed a
keystroke early. `ui-review` reproduced the right-hand column
independently against a dev server running this change.

That mattered more after #282, which made the panel reachable under
`next dev` at the loopback address rather than at `localhost` alone.

What this costs is three things gated on the same flag: the Dev Tools
menu and its trigger, the cache badge, and the build-activity pill, so
there is no compiling or rendering feedback in dev. Errors are not among
them -- that is Next's separate issues badge.

Which is also the boundary, and it is stated in the comment rather than
left to be found. The issues badge is the same portal in the same place
and focusable in the same way; it appears on the first logged error, and
this application produces one itself from `sendChatMessage`'s `catch` on
any stack with no chat service. So this narrows when dev disagrees with
production without ending it, and #290 carries the general form: nothing
tells `ui-review` that a keyboard journey needs a production build.

No test. The effect is DOM tab order on a running dev server, and there
is no seam to assert it through: `devIndicators` is a DefinePlugin
constant consumed inside the compiled devtools bundle, with no analogue
to the `blockCrossSiteDEV` call that `next-dev-origins.test.ts` uses.
Vitest cannot start a dev server -- one per `distDir` via `.next/dev/lock`
-- and the journeys run against `next start`, where the indicator does
not exist. Asserting the config key would be the declaration check
`AGENTS.md` rejects. `verifier` looked for a seam and found none.

Filed from this work: #289 (on the phone sheet, Send appears at the
coordinates the launcher was tapped) and #290.

Refs #277
EOF
